chapters.title: Modern Microbiology for Allied Health Professions: An Overview

questions.stem: Which of these items can a genome be made of?
questions.answerRationale: A genome is nucleic acid - DNA or RNA - never lipid, carbohydrate, or protein.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most accurate/complete description of a genome?

options.text: All the nucleic acids in a cell.
All the chromosomes in the nucleus of a cell.
All the proteins (enzymes) of a genome creature.
The DNA or RNA contents that carry the genetic blueprint of a creature.

questions.answerRationale: The genome is the DNA or RNA content carrying the genetic blueprint; "all nucleic acids" is too broad (includes non-genomic RNA) and "chromosomes in a nucleus" excludes prokaryotes, organelles, and acellular microbes.

questions.stem: Which of these types of genome creatures may perform?
questions.answerRationale: Acellular genome creatures (viruses, etc.) cannot independently maintain homeostasis, grow, or transform energy - the one trait shared across all genome creatures, cellular or not, is that their genetic material can replicate, mutate, and evolve.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is associated with all microbes?

options.text: All microbes infect other organisms and cause diseases.
All microbes are invisible to the naked eye.

questions.answerRationale: Chapter 1 frames essentially every microbe as a genome creature; prions are the deliberate, separately-flagged exception, not a reason to abandon the general rule this early question is testing.

questions.stem: Which of the following agents is not considered a microbe?
questions.answerRationale: A mushroom is the macroscopic, visible fruiting body of a fungus - unlike the microscopic yeasts/molds, or the "metazoan microbes" (worms, arthropods) this book still classifies as microbes, a mushroom itself is not treated as one.

questions.stem: Which of the following microbes is also a microorganism?
questions.answerRationale: A bacterium is a true cellular, living organism - a "microorganism." Satellites, virusoids, viroids, and viruses are all acellular and lack independent metabolism.

questions.stem: Which of the following propositions in microbiology has been proven beyond doubt?

options.text: All acellular microbes depend on cellular microbes.
All acellular microbes evolved from cellular microbes.
All cellular microbes evolved from acellular microbes.

questions.answerRationale: Every acellular microbe is an obligate parasite of a host cell (proven, observable fact); whether acellular life evolved before or after cellular life is still a debated, unproven hypothesis.

questions.stem: Which of the following virus particles is a virion?

options.text: It can infect its host cell without any other necessities.

questions.answerRationale: A virion is defined functionally as the complete, independently infectious viral particle - envelope, genome type, and capsid nakedness are all just structural variants, not what makes something a virion.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a satellite (type of virus)?

options.text: It does not need a helper virus to infect a host cell.
It has a DNA or an RNA genome and a capsid.
It uses the capsid of a helper virus.
It has a circular ssRNA genome.

questions.answerRationale: A satellite has its own genome AND its own capsid (just not its own replication enzymes, which is why it needs a helper virus); using the helper's capsid instead of its own is what specifically defines a virusoid, not satellites generally.

questions.stem: A virusoid has a circular RNA genome and a stolen capsid. Which of these groups does it belong to?
questions.answerRationale: A virusoid (circular RNA genome + stolen capsid) is a subtype of satellite - the type that borrows its capsid instead of encoding one.

questions.stem: Why are viroids different from viruses and satellites, including virusoids?

options.text: Viroid genomes are made of a short circular ssRNA.
Viroid genomes lack genes, yet viroids do not require a helper virus to infect their host cells.

questions.answerRationale: Both viroids and virusoids are non-coding RNAs, so lacking genes isn't unique to viroids - what sets viroids apart is that they replicate with zero helper virus at all, using only host enzymes.

questions.stem: How are plasmids different from viruses?

options.text: They can move from one host cell to another.
They can have a DNA or an RNA genome.
They do not have a capsid.

questions.answerRationale: Plasmids are naked DNA/RNA with no protein coat at all, unlike viruses which always package their genome in a capsid.

questions.stem: Plasmids are usually not found in the cells of which of these creatures?

options.text: Higher eukarya, such as vertebrate animals.

questions.answerRationale: Plasmids are a hallmark of microbial genetics (bacteria, archaea, and even some protists/fungi) but are essentially absent from complex multicellular eukaryotes like vertebrates.

questions.stem: Why “Mobile DNA” is a more appropriate name for transposons.

options.text: They may or may not have genes.
They are not found in RNA genomes.
They cannot move out of the host cell.
They can move from one location in the host genome to another.

questions.answerRationale: "Mobile DNA" describes exactly what a transposon does - it relocates from one position in the host genome to another, rather than moving between cells or organisms.

questions.stem: Transposons (mobile DNA) are not expected be found in the genome of which of these genome creatures?

options.text: RNA viruses, RNA satellites, and viroids.

questions.answerRationale: Transposons are DNA elements; they are not found in genomes made entirely of RNA (RNA viruses, RNA satellites, viroids).

questions.stem: Which of these is a prion?

options.text: It is found in the prokaryotic cells.
It has a very tiny RNA genome lacking genes.

questions.answerRationale: A prion is specifically an abnormal, misfolded ("mutated" in the sense of altered conformation) version of a normal cellular protein - just "a protein" (A) is too generic to define it, and prions have no genome at all (ruling out D).

questions.stem: Prions lack a genome, yet they cause disease in animals, including human subjects. How do they cause disease?

options.text: They destroy other proteins of the affected cells.
They bind and destroy the genome of the affected cells.
They convert normal cellular prion proteins into insoluble, abnormal prion proteins.

questions.answerRationale: Prions cause disease by templating their misfolded shape onto normal cellular prion protein (PrP), converting it into more of the insoluble, abnormal form - a chain reaction, not by attacking other proteins or a genome.

questions.stem: Which of the following organisms can be infected by some species of viruses?
questions.answerRationale: Viruses infect representatives of essentially every domain and kingdom of cellular life - bacteria, archaea, fungi, protozoa, plants, and animals alike.

questions.stem: Microbes can infect animals, plants, and other microbes. Which of these microbes infect or take advantage of viruses?
questions.answerRationale: Satellites are obligately dependent on a helper virus for replication enzymes, literally exploiting it; transposons are also known to hitch inside and move via viral genomes.

questions.stem: Which of the following most certainly describes a prokaryotic cell?

options.text: It has a nucleoid but not a karyon.

questions.answerRationale: Having a nucleoid instead of a true membrane-bound nucleus (karyon) is the one defining, always-true criterion of a prokaryotic cell - unlike a cell wall (Mycoplasma lacks one) or "many ribosomes," which are not strict universals.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely a eukaryotic cell?

options.text: It is smaller than prokaryotic cells.
Its genome is in an organelle surrounded by a membrane.
It has transposons in its genome and can be infected by viruses and plasmids.

questions.answerRationale: Housing the genome inside a membrane-bound organelle (the nucleus) is the defining eukaryotic trait - eukaryotes have a "karyon," not a "nucleoid," and are generally larger, not smaller, than prokaryotes.

questions.stem: Which of these classification hierarchies is a domain?

options.text: It is made of related Kingdoms.
It is made of related Families.
It is made of related Phyla.
It is made of related Orders.
It is made of related Genera.

questions.answerRationale: Standard taxonomic hierarchy runs Domain > Kingdom > Phylum > Class > Order > Family > Genus > Species, so a domain is made of related kingdoms.

questions.stem: Which of these environments may one find prokaryotes?

options.text: The deepest ocean trenches and the highest mountain peaks.
Body surfaces and inside the cells of eukaryotic organisms.
The driest deserts and the permafrost of the tundra.
Boiling geysers and thermal vents of the seafloor.

questions.answerRationale: Prokaryotes are famously ubiquitous extremophiles and generalists, found in every environment listed - deep trenches, mountain peaks, body surfaces, deserts, permafrost, and thermal vents alike.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements on prokaryotes is CORRECT?

options.text: Most species of bacteria are pathogenic.
Archaea are not found on human body surfaces.
Pathogenic archaea have never been reported in humans.
All archaea live in extreme environments such as acid lakes and salt flats.

questions.answerRationale: Most bacterial species are not pathogenic and archaea are found on human body surfaces (e.g. gut methanogens) - but no archaeon has ever been conclusively established as a human pathogen, a genuinely notable and often-tested fact.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups of eukaryotes have metazoan microbes?
questions.answerRationale: The book's term "metazoan microbes" (multicellular animal-type organisms still studied in microbiology) specifically covers worms and arthropods.

questions.stem: Which of these algal species would be more likely to infect other organisms?

options.text: One that lacks chloroplasts and cannot conduct photosynthesis.
One that has chloroplasts and can conduct photosynthesis.
One that produces toxins in warm and polluted water.
One that lives in freshwater, mud, and moist soil.

questions.answerRationale: An alga that has lost its chloroplasts and photosynthetic ability must get nutrients some other way, pushing it toward a heterotrophic, parasitic lifestyle - exactly the pattern seen in Prototheca, the one algal genus with genuine animal pathogens.

questions.stem: Which of these fungi is a yeast?

options.text: It decomposes dead plants and animals or infects live plants and animals.
It synthesizes antibiotics used in treating some microbial infections.
It produces toxins that can affect human health.
It has a thread-like multicellular structure.

questions.answerRationale: Yeast is defined by its unicellular growth form; the thread-like multicellular form (D) describes mold, not yeast.

questions.stem: Why are protozoa called tiny animals?

options.text: They can be single-celled or a colony of several identical cells.
Their cells lack a cell wall and can eat solid food particles.
They thrive only in water or moist places.

questions.answerRationale: Protozoa are called "tiny animals" because, like animal cells, they lack a cell wall and can actively ingest solid food particles (phagocytosis) - not because of size, habitat, or pathogenicity.

questions.stem: Which of these is a lichen?

options.text: It is a symbiosis (live together) of one or more fungi and an alga or a cyanobacterium.
It is a symbiosis (live together) of one or more fungi and a protozoan or slime mold.
It is an important food source for animals in the polar region
It is a colony of cells that recycle soil nutrients.

questions.answerRationale: A lichen is the textbook symbiosis of a fungus with a photosynthetic partner - an alga or a cyanobacterium.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is CORRECT about worms that are described in microbiology textbooks?

options.text: They lack a body cavity or have a false body cavity.
They are either long-worms or short-worms.

questions.answerRationale: Flatworms are acoelomate and nematodes are pseudocoelomate - "lacking a body cavity or having only a false one" is broadly true of the worm groups covered here, unlike the other options which are simply false (not all worms are parasitic, and worms are animals, not Protists).

questions.stem: Which of these arthropods (joint-footed animals) is considered a vector?

options.text: It burrows into human skin and lays eggs there, causing inflammation.
It transfers pathogenic microbes from other animals to humans.
It does not desiccate if placed in the open air.
It is usually a spider or a crustacean.

questions.answerRationale: A "vector" is defined by its role in disease transmission - an organism that carries a pathogen from one host (often an animal reservoir) to another, here to humans.

sections.heading: The species concept, population, and strain

questions.stem: Which of the following is a natural definition of a species?

options.text: A group of acellular agents that infect a particular cell type and share some distinctive characteristics.
A population of prokaryotic organisms with some similar distinctive characteristics.
A population of male and female organisms that breeds fertile offspring.

questions.answerRationale: The classic biological species concept - a population that interbreeds and produces fertile offspring - is the natural, general definition of species, but it only applies to sexually reproducing organisms.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a helpful definition (a pathologist can apply it) of a bacterial species?

options.text: A population of male and female organisms that breeds fertile offspring.
A population of prokaryotic organisms with some similar distinctive characteristics.
A group of acellular agents that infect a particular cell type and share some distinctive characteristics.

questions.answerRationale: Bacteria don't reproduce sexually, so the biological species concept is useless to a pathologist; the practical definition actually applied to bacteria is a population sharing similar distinctive characteristics.

questions.stem: Which of these is a strain?

options.text: A microbe that can infect humans or animals.
All the individuals of a species living in an environment.
A population of a species that is genetically slightly different from another population of the same species.

questions.answerRationale: A strain is a genetically slightly different population within the same species - not a different species, not a definition of pathogenicity, and not simply "a population."

questions.stem: Which of these organizations sets the rules for naming and approves the species names for prokaryotic microbes?
questions.answerRationale: The Bacteriological Code is the rulebook (and its governing body) that sets and approves species names for prokaryotes, distinct from ICZN/ICBN (animals/plants) and ICTV (viruses).

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an ICTV-approved rule for naming an acellular microbe?

options.text: The second and subsequent words of the name should not be capitalized.
The first letter of the name must be a capital letter.
The name must be spelled as ICTV spells it.
The entire name must be italicized.

questions.answerRationale: ICTV rules do NOT allow abbreviating an official virus species name - that is reserved for informal common names like "HSV-1"; capitalization, spelling, and full italicization of the species name are all real ICTV rules.

questions.stem: Which of the following virus names (mentioned in the sentences) is a correctly formatted scientific name?

options.text: The herpes simplex virus type 1 has a DNA genome.
The fever blister virus may cause a latent infection of some neural ganglia.

questions.answerRationale: "Human alphaherpesvirus 1" is the properly formatted, italicized ICTV species name; HSV-1, "herpes simplex virus type 1," and "the fever blister virus" are all informal common names.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT an approved rule for naming a cellular microbe?

options.text: The entire name should be italicized.
The second word of the name must be capitalized.
The first letter of the genus name must be capitalized.
The name should be spelled as approved by ICZN or ICBN.

questions.answerRationale: The species epithet (second word) of a binomial name is never capitalized - only the genus name's first letter is.

questions.stem: The common name of the bacterium that causes gonorrhea (a sexually transmitted disease) is gonococcus. Which of the following is the correct scientific species name of the same organism? Note: Assume that all the names are italicized.
questions.answerRationale: "Neisseria gonorrhoeae" is the correctly formatted full binomial species name; the genus alone, the epithet alone, and a capitalized epithet are all incomplete or wrong.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacterial species names (shown in sentences) is a correctly formatted scientific name? Note: Assume that all the names are italicized.

options.text: Staphylococcus Aureus is a pathogenic bacterium.
Staphylococcus aureus can cause wound infections.
Some strains of staphylococcus aureus secrete exotoxins.

questions.answerRationale: "Staphylococcus aureus" is properly capitalized (genus) and lowercase (species epithet) and used as a full binomial - the other options either give the genus alone, wrongly capitalize "Aureus," or fail to capitalize the genus.

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of these statements is CORRECT about the bacterial species names Streptococcus pneumoniae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae? Note: Assume that all the names are italicised.

options.text: They are different names of the same species.
They are different names of the same genus.
They are names of three different species.
They are names of three different genera.

questions.answerRationale: Despite sharing the species epithet "pneumoniae" (all three cause pneumonia), Streptococcus, Klebsiella, and Mycoplasma are three entirely different genera - the deeper, more specific insight the challenge question is testing, beyond the more trivial fact that they are also three different species.

questions.stem: An isolate of a microbe is currently identified as X1003878E2014. Which of these describes this isolate?

options.text: It is a virus or a subviral agent.
The isolate been identified and characterized.
The isolate has not yet been fully characterized.

questions.answerRationale: A bare alphanumeric code like this is a placeholder isolate designation used before a microbe has been fully characterized and assigned a formal name.

questions.stem: Which of these is (a) the highest hierarchy of classification of viruses, and (b) which of these is the most commonly found highest hierarchy of the classified viruses?
questions.answerRationale: In this book's simplified framework, Family is the highest formal rank used for virus classification, while Genus is in practice the highest rank actually assigned to most classified viruses.

questions.stem: What is the central assumption of phylogenetic classification?

options.text: Populations evolve so rapidly that they cannot be grouped into species.
Taxonomy (the science of classification) is an arbitrary discipline.
All lower taxa within a higher taxon share a common ancestor.
All the ancestral groups of existing organisms are extinct.

questions.answerRationale: Phylogenetic classification rests on the assumption that all lower taxa nested within a higher taxon share a common ancestor - the core premise of tree-based, evolutionary classification.

questions.stem: Which of these is CORRECT about microbes in antiquity?

options.text: People of antiquity visualized some microbes.
People in antiquity cultivated and used certain microbes.
People of antiquity described and drew pictures of some microbes.
People of antiquity never used, visualized, or described any microbes.

questions.answerRationale: Ancient peoples couldn't see or describe microbes without microscopes, but they did cultivate and exploit them unknowingly - fermenting bread, beer, wine, and cheese using yeasts and bacteria.

sections.heading: Chemical evolution and the origin of life

questions.stem: Which of these scientists demonstrated that amino acids can be synthesized in a glass bulb containing a mixture of hydrogen, ammonia, methane, and water vapor, and then zapped with electricity sparks?
questions.answerRationale: This is the classic Miller-Urey experiment (1952), sparking a gas mixture of H2, NH3, CH4, and H2O to synthesize amino acids.

questions.stem: If life evolved from inorganic chemicals through several stages to a cell, which of these is the third of the five stages from the beginning?

options.text: Small organic compounds, such as amino acids and fatty acids, are synthesized.
Protocells are created due to the fusion of DNA or RNA and lipid micelles.
Small molecules such as NH3, CH4, H2, H2O, etc., existed in nature.
Macromolecules such as DNA and RNA were synthesized.
Lipid vesicles/liposomes were formed from fatty acids.

questions.answerRationale: The five stages run: (1) small inorganic molecules exist naturally, (2) small organic compounds (amino/fatty acids) form, (3) macromolecules like DNA and RNA are synthesized, (4) lipid vesicles form from fatty acids, (5) protocells form from DNA/RNA plus lipid micelles - making macromolecule synthesis the third stage.

questions.stem: Philosophers and naturalists developed knowledge by all the following methods EXCEPT by ________.
questions.answerRationale: Making and testing hypotheses is the hallmark of the modern scientific method, not the older philosophical/descriptive approach of inquiring, reasoning, debating, and theorizing.

questions.stem: Which of these is the descriptive method of acquiring knowledge?

options.text: Inquiring, reasoning, critiquing, debating, discussing, and theorizing.
Observing, asking questions, and making, testing, and accepting/rejecting hypotheses.
Observing and collecting data to understand the underlying principles without manipulating the study materials.

questions.answerRationale: The descriptive method is observation and data collection to understand underlying patterns without manipulating the study material - as opposed to the scientific method's active hypothesis testing.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the theory of spontaneous generation support?

options.text: Cells are the structural and functional units of all organisms.
The eukaryotic cells evolved from the prokaryotic cells.
A cell may originate only from a preexisting cell.
A mouse can be generated in a pile of garbage.

questions.answerRationale: Spontaneous generation is literally the pre-scientific belief that living things (like a mouse) can arise directly from non-living matter (like a pile of garbage) - the opposite of biogenesis, which the cell theory (option A) and C both actually refute.

questions.stem: Ignaz Semmelweis observed that more women who delivered their babies in the hospitals suffered from puerperal fever than those who delivered at home under the guidance of midwives. Which of the following hypotheses would Semmelweis have made (before he tested the hypothesis)?

options.text: There are more germs in hospitals than in households.
Hospital physicians do not transfer germs from patient to patient.
Midwives are more proficient in child delivery than hospital physicians.
Women who deliver babies at home are healthier than those who deliver babies in hospitals.

questions.answerRationale: Before testing, and without the modern language of germ theory, Semmelweis's working hypothesis was that something in the hospital environment - "more germs" in modern terms - was the source of the excess puerperal fever, a precursor to his eventual conclusion about doctors carrying it from patient to patient.

questions.stem: If Ignaz Semmelweis were testing his hypothesis (hospital physicians transfer germs from patient to patient). Which of these can be considered his control sample?

options.text: Doctors washed their hands before assisting with childbirth.
Doctors did not wash their hands before assisting with childbirth.
The number of women who suffered from puerperal fever after assisted childbirth.
The number of women who had not suffered from puerperal fever after assisted childbirth.

questions.answerRationale: In his hand-washing experiment, the intervention was doctors washing their hands; "not washing hands" was the pre-existing standard practice serving as the baseline/control against which the effect of hand-washing was measured.

questions.stem: In terms of optics, what was the critical difference between D'Armati’s eyeglasses and Leeuwenhoek’s microscopes?

options.text: Types of frames used in the construction.

questions.answerRationale: Leeuwenhoek's microscopes had a mechanism for adjusting the distance between lens and specimen to bring it into sharp focus at extreme magnification; eyeglasses are simple, fixed-focus corrective lenses with no such mechanism.

questions.stem: Which of the following discoveries was made by Pasteur?

options.text: Certain microbes can grow in the absence of oxygen (i.e., in the absence of air).
A bacterium causes the pebrine disease of silkworms.
Heat-killed rabies viruses can be used as vaccines.

questions.answerRationale: Pasteur demonstrated that certain microbes (he coined the terms aerobic/anaerobic) can grow without oxygen - the pebrine agent is actually a protozoan/microsporidian, not a bacterium, and it was yeast that caused fermentation while separate contaminating bacteria, not yeast, caused wine souring.

questions.stem: Why did the process of pasteurization (i.e., heating grape juice at 60 °C for 30 minutes before fermentation) solve the problem of wine-souring?

options.text: The process killed yeast but not bacteria.
The process killed bacteria but not yeasts.
The process removed the acids that soured the wine.
The process concentrated alcohol and reduced the acids in the vat.

questions.answerRationale: Heating the grape juice before fermentation killed the contaminating spoilage bacteria responsible for souring, while a controlled yeast culture was still used afterward to carry out the desired alcoholic fermentation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an article of the Koch’s postulates?

options.text: The same microbe must be present in all cases of the disease in question.
The microbe must be isolated from the infected organisms as a pure culture.
A test animal inoculated with the microbe from a pure culture should develop the disease.
All microbe species (including the test microbe) affecting the test animal should be isolated in pure cultures.

questions.answerRationale: Koch's fourth postulate requires re-isolating the SAME test microbe from the experimentally infected animal, not isolating every microbe species present in that animal.

questions.stem: Why was Pasteur unable to prove the germ theory of disease?

options.text: He was not applying the Koch’s postulates.
He used liquid culture media to grow microbes.
Because Agostino Bassi proved the theory before Pasteur.
Because he used semi-solid culture media to grow microbes.

questions.answerRationale: Pasteur worked primarily with liquid broth cultures, which mix multiple microbial species together and make it essentially impossible to reliably isolate a single, pure causative organism - the technical gap that Koch's solid-media pure-culture technique later closed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a contribution of Robert Koch?

options.text: Designing filters that remove bacteria from a liquid.
Identifying Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the causative agent of tuberculosis.
Reporting that the bacterium Bacillus anthracis produces highly stable endospores.

questions.answerRationale: The bacteria-removing porcelain filter is credited to Charles Chamberland, a colleague of Pasteur's - not Koch, whose real contributions include identifying M. tuberculosis, describing B. anthracis endospores, and advancing sterilization and water-safety practices.

sections.heading: The three golden ages of microbiology

questions.stem: The Second Golden Age of microbiology spanned _________, and one of the most important discoveries of the period is _______.
questions.answerRationale: The Second Golden Age of microbiology (roughly 1940-1970, the post-WWII era) is marked by advances like the electron microscope, coming after the first "classic bacteriology" golden age and before the post-genomic era.

questions.stem: Some scientists and their discoveries are listed below. One of the items is mispaired. Which one of these is mispaired?

options.text: Von Behring and Kitasato: Humoral immunity, and antitoxin (antibodies).
Pasteur, Koch, and Roux: Attenuation of microbes to produce a vaccine.
Jules Bordet: Infectious agents that pass through a bacterial filter.
Fleming and Domagk: Antimicrobial chemotherapeutic agents.

questions.answerRationale: Discovering filterable infectious agents (viruses, via tobacco mosaic virus) is credited to Ivanovsky and Beijerinck, not Jules Bordet, who is instead known for discovering the complement system and Bordetella pertussis.

questions.stem: Who discovered that DNA is the carrier of heredity (i.e., genetic information) of cellular organisms?
questions.answerRationale: Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty (1944) were the first to experimentally show that DNA, not protein, is the transforming/hereditary material in bacteria - years before Hershey-Chase confirmed it further, and well before Watson/Crick/Franklin worked out DNA's structure.

questions.stem: What are the beginning and end of the post-genomic era of microbiology’s golden ages?
questions.answerRationale: The post-genomic golden age of microbiology runs from about 1970 to the present, driven by molecular biology and genome sequencing.

questions.stem: The microbiology course curriculum, given by the American Society of Microbiology, requires us to discuss all these areas of microbiology. Which area discusses microbial genomes, genes, gene expression, and gene expression regulation?
questions.answerRationale: "Biological information flow" is the ASM curriculum area covering the central dogma - genomes, genes, gene expression, and its regulation.

questions.stem: Which of the following UNUSUAL root problems did the discoveries and inventions in the field of microbiology contribute to?

options.text: Lack of food safety and food security.
Shortage of clean and safe drinking water.
The rapid growth of the human population.

questions.answerRationale: Microbiology's biggest historical win - crushing infectious-disease mortality - is also, paradoxically, a root driver of the rapid human population growth now straining every other resource, making it the "unusual" contribution among these choices.

questions.stem: Challenge question: The following are some of the most pressing problems our society is facing today. Which of the issues can be exacerbated by microbes?
questions.answerRationale: Microbial pathogens (like the amphibian chytrid fungus and bat white-nose syndrome fungus) are among the most directly documented drivers of modern biodiversity loss.

chapters.title: Microcopy and Structure of the Cell

questions.stem: If a meter is about 1.09 yards, about how many cm make an inch?
questions.answerRationale: 1 m ≈ 1.09 yd = 39.24 in, so 100 cm / 39.24 in ≈ 2.55 cm per inch.

questions.stem: The gross weight of an aspirin tablet is 0.5 grams; it contains 325 mg of the drug aspirin (the rest are binders such as cellulose, cornstarch, and coloring). How many mg of an aspirin tablet (gross weight) contain 100 mg of the drug (pure aspirin)?
questions.answerRationale: 0.5 g gross tablet has 325 mg active drug, so 100 mg active drug scales to 500 × (100/325) ≈ 154 mg gross weight.

questions.stem: A person's fasting sugar level is 120 mg per deciliter. You have 2 mL of the person's blood. How many mg of sugar does the sample contain?
questions.answerRationale: 120 mg/dL = 120 mg per 100 mL, so 2 mL contains 120 × (2/100) = 2.4 mg of sugar.

questions.stem: In a brightfield LM, a light beam passes through each of the following items. Which is the second of the items?
questions.answerRationale: Light in a brightfield LM travels: diaphragm, then condenser lens, then the specimen, then objective lens, then ocular lens, then the eye - making the condenser lens second.

questions.stem: The resolution capacity of commonly used LMs equipped with glass lenses is about _____, mainly because ______.

options.text: 5 nm, thin glass lenses can be made these days
50 nm/ glass and air have identical refractive indices
200 nm/ the wavelength of visible light is 400-700 nm
500 nm/ multiple glass lenses are used as the ocular and objective lenses

questions.answerRationale: Glass-lens light microscopes resolve to about 200 nm because that is roughly the diffraction limit set by the 400-700 nm wavelength range of visible light.

questions.stem: Staining of the samples solves which of the limitations of the technology used in light microscopy?

options.text: Glass lenses (and the biological specimens) are transparent.
Light bends when passing from air to water and vice versa.
The wavelength of visible light is 400-700 nm.

questions.answerRationale: Staining solves the problem that glass lenses and unstained biological specimens are both essentially transparent and colorless, giving almost no contrast.

questions.stem: Immersion oil is used ______.

options.text: only if the specimen is unstained
if the power of the objective lens is 50 or less
to minimize the amount of light emerging from the specimen to enter the objective lens
to maximize the amount of light emerging from the specimen to enter the objective lens

questions.answerRationale: Immersion oil matches the refractive index of glass, preventing light from bending away at the specimen-air-lens boundary and instead maximizing the light collected by a high-power objective.

questions.stem: Which of these glass lenses has the highest power?

options.text: The lens that has the shortest focal length (f).
The lens is made of quartz.

questions.answerRationale: Lens power is inversely related to focal length - the shorter the focal length, the higher the magnifying power.

questions.stem: The size of the image created by a light microscope (LM) of a 3-micrometer bacterium is 1.5 mm. What is the magnification (in x)?
questions.answerRationale: Magnification = image size / actual size = 1.5 mm / 0.003 mm (3 micrometers) = 500x.

questions.stem: One used a 50x objective lens and a 10x ocular lens to examine a bacterium 0.5 micrometers in length. What will be the size of the image of the bacterium? Note: First, calculate the total magnification.
questions.answerRationale: Total magnification = 50x × 10x = 500x; 0.5 micrometers × 500 = 250 micrometers.

questions.stem: The image of a virus particle appeared 6 mm in diameter to a viewer using a microscope. The image of the virus particle was magnified 50,000x. What is the actual diameter of the virus particle (in nm)?
questions.answerRationale: 6 mm = 6,000,000 nm; divided by the 50,000x magnification gives an actual diameter of 120 nm.

questions.stem: You want to count the fraction of live (motile) spermatozoa relative to non-motile spermatozoa of male mice. The mice were previously treated with polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB), a toxic substance released by plastic materials. Which of the following methods would you use? Note: LM- light microscopes.

options.text: Put a drop of the diluted semen on a glass slide and examine under a brightfield LM.
Put a drop of the diluted semen on a glass slide and examine under a dark-field LM.
Make a smear of the diluted semen on a glass slide, stain with iodine, and examine under a phase-contrast microscope.
Make a smear of the diluted semen on a glass slide, stain with hematoxylin, and examine under a differential interference contrast microscope.

questions.answerRationale: Assessing motility requires observing live, unstained cells - staining or fixing (as in the other three options) kills the cells - and dark-field microscopy is specifically suited to giving unstained live specimens like sperm strong contrast.

questions.stem: Which of these is a differential interference contrast microscope?

options.text: It uses polarized light and prisms.
It has an opaque barrier in its condenser lens.
The image it creates appears on a dark background.

questions.answerRationale: A differential interference contrast (DIC) microscope is defined by its use of polarized light split through prisms to generate contrast from subtle optical path differences.

questions.stem: Why does the image of a specimen appear to glow when examined using a simple fluorescence microscope or a confocal microscope?

options.text: Both these microscopes use UV light as the light source.
Both these microscopes scan the specimen to create the image.
Both these microscopes require the specimen to be labeled with an antibody.
Both these microscopes require the specimen to be stained with a fluorochrome.

questions.answerRationale: The one thing a simple fluorescence microscope and a confocal microscope both require is that the specimen be stained with a fluorochrome, which absorbs light at one wavelength and re-emits ("glows") at a longer one.

questions.stem: Which of these statements is INCORRECT about confocal microscopes?

options.text: The specimen must be tilted and scanned slice by slice
This type of microscope cannot be used to examine live cells.
The specimens must be stained with one or more fluorescent dyes.
A laser source must be used to excite the fluorescent dyes on the specimens.
The final image of the specimen must be assembled using computer software.

questions.answerRationale: A major advantage of confocal microscopy is that it CAN be used to examine live cells, unlike electron microscopy - making the claim that it cannot the false statement here.

questions.stem: Electron microscopes (EMs) can magnify more than 100,000x while resolving to 0.05 to 2.5 nm. Which of these is the main reason behind this high capacity of resolution?

options.text: EMs use metal solenoids as lenses.
For EMs, the specimens are thinly sliced and stained with metal salts.
EMs use an electron beam (wavelength of 0.004-0.012 nm) for imaging.
EMs create images of specimens on a fluorescent screen or using computer software.

questions.answerRationale: Resolution is fundamentally limited by the wavelength used for imaging, and an electron beam's wavelength (0.004-0.012 nm) is thousands of times shorter than visible light's, which is the core physical reason for EM's vastly superior resolution.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT about SEM but not TEM?

options.text: Energy used for imaging is an electron beam (not a photon beam).
The specimens should be placed on a metal grid (not a glass slide).
The lenses used are metal solenoids (not curved, polished glass).
The specimens must be fixed and coated with nanoparticles.
The images created are always black-and-white.

questions.answerRationale: SEM specimens must be fixed and coated with a thin layer of metal (e.g. gold-palladium) to make the surface conductive for scanning, while TEM instead requires ultrathin sectioning and heavy-metal staining for electron transmission - the other listed traits (electron beam, metal grids, solenoid lenses, grayscale images) are shared by both.

questions.stem: Some electrons passed through the specimen, but some were reflected because they hit the heavy metal ions used to stain the specimen. What type of EM is being used for this experiment?
questions.answerRationale: Electrons passing through a thin specimen, with some scattered by heavy-metal stain, is the classic transmission-based image formation of a TEM.

questions.stem: Which of the following microscopes may NOT provide a 3-D image of the specimen?
questions.answerRationale: A standard TEM image is a 2-D transmission projection through an ultrathin slice - not inherently 3-D like confocal z-stacks, DIC's relief effect, or SEM's surface topography.

questions.stem: Which of the components of a bacterial flagellum provides it with motility by acting as a proton-motive motor?
questions.answerRationale: The basal body houses the rotary motor complex driven by the proton motive force, which is what actually powers flagellar rotation.

questions.stem: The basal body of a bacterium is rotating counterclockwise. What is this bacterium doing at this moment?

options.text: It is on a run (moving forward).

questions.answerRationale: Counterclockwise rotation of the flagellar motor bundles the flagella together for smooth forward swimming (a "run"); clockwise rotation causes them to fly apart into a tumble.

questions.stem: Which of the following flagellum types would cause the bacterium to move like a corkscrew?
questions.answerRationale: A single polar (monotrichous) flagellum rotating like a propeller drives the cell forward in a corkscrew-like spinning motion.

questions.stem: Which of the following pili is most likely involved in electron transport?
questions.answerRationale: Bacterial nanowires are literally the structure certain bacteria (like Geobacter) use for extracellular electron transport.

questions.stem: Which of these allows a bacterium to conduct conjugation?
questions.answerRationale: Sex pili form the mating bridge that allows DNA transfer between bacteria during conjugation.

questions.stem: There are many species of bacteria in the healthy human body. Among them, pathogenic species often have flagella, pili, and glycocalyx, whereas non-pathogenic species usually lack them. Which of these terms is used to call these structures of pathogenic bacteria?

options.text: Spreading Factors Bacterial structure: Glycocalyx (slime, capsule, biofilm, etc.)

questions.answerRationale: Structures like flagella, pili, and glycocalyx that contribute to a pathogen's ability to cause disease are collectively called virulence factors.

questions.stem: Which of these bacterial cell exudates is considered a biofilm?

options.text: It is shared by many members of the species.
It is made primarily of polysaccharides.
It is very loosely attached to the cell.
It is made primarily of polypeptides.
It is tightly attached to the cells.

questions.answerRationale: A biofilm is a structured, often multi-species community shared by many members of a bacterial population, distinguishing it from an individual cell's own loosely- or tightly-bound capsule/slime layer.

questions.stem: About 50% of all bacterial species secrete capsules, and up to 80% of pathogenic bacteria secrete a biofilm. Which of these abilities is NOT associated with a biofilm of pathogenic bacteria?

options.text: Preventing predation by protozoan and slime molds.
Helping with adhering to tissues and inanimate surfaces.
Settling on live tissues more efficiently than inanimate objects in the body.

questions.answerRationale: Biofilms protect against desiccation, harmful chemicals, and predation, and help bacteria adhere to surfaces - but there is no established rule that they settle more efficiently on living tissue than on inanimate objects (biofilms famously colonize catheters and pipes just as readily).

questions.stem: Which of these components of a peptidoglycan (PG) cell wall is made entirely of amino acids?
questions.answerRationale: The peptide cross-linking chains of peptidoglycan are made entirely of amino acids; murein, NAG, and NAM all include sugar components.

questions.stem: Which of the following bacteria has a thin cell wall hidden in the periplasmic space created by two membranes?

options.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a G(-) shapeless bacterium.

questions.answerRationale: Gram-negative bacteria like E. coli have a thin peptidoglycan layer tucked into the periplasmic space between the inner (plasma) membrane and the outer membrane.

sections.heading: Bacterial structure: The plasma membrane and the envelope

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT found in the bacterial plasma membrane?

options.text: Proteins, including receptors and transport proteins.

questions.answerRationale: True sterols with a hydrocarbon tail are largely a eukaryotic membrane feature; most bacteria instead use hopanoids as a functional substitute (Mycoplasma, which incorporates host sterols, is the well-known exception).

questions.stem: Of the prokaryotes, ___________ type of bacteria have two membranes, and _________ bacteria gave two cell walls?
questions.answerRationale: Gram-negative bacteria have two membranes (inner and outer); Actinobacteria effectively have two wall-like layers (peptidoglycan plus an outer mycolic acid layer).

questions.stem: All the membranes of the cell have two lipid layers (leaves). Where in the membrane of a G(-) bacterium may one find lipopolysaccharides (LPS)?

options.text: Inner leaf of the inner membrane.
Outer leaf of the inner membrane.
Inner leaf of the outer membrane (envelope).
Outer leaf of the outer membrane (envelope).

questions.answerRationale: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is found exclusively in the outer leaflet of the outer membrane, facing the external environment - the defining feature of the Gram-negative envelope.

sections.heading: Bacterial structures: The endotoxins (PG, LPS, and LTA) and mycolic acid

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about bacterial endotoxin is CORRECT?

options.text: They are secreted by live bacterial cells.
They are toxic because they kill human cells.
They are toxic because they bind receptors and activate macrophages.

questions.answerRationale: Endotoxin (LPS) is toxic because it binds receptors like TLR4 on macrophages and triggers an overwhelming inflammatory cytokine response - it is not itself a directly cytotoxic protein, and it is released mainly on cell lysis, not actively secreted by live cells.

questions.stem: Some actinobacteria, such as mycobacteria, have a mycolic acid layer on their outermost surfaces. Mycolic acid is made of lipids. Which of these statements is correct about these bacteria?

options.text: They are easier to treat with antibiotics.

questions.answerRationale: The waxy, hydrophobic mycolic acid layer makes these bacteria notoriously difficult to stain by ordinary methods, requiring specialized acid-fast staining - and far from being nonpathogenic or easy to treat, mycolic-acid bacteria like Mycobacterium are classic hard-to-treat pathogens.

questions.stem: Many pathogenic bacteria produce exotoxins. Which of these correctly describes an exotoxin?

options.text: They are part of the outer membranes and cell wall of bacteria.
They can be made of lipids and polysaccharides.
They are released only by dead bacteria.

questions.answerRationale: Exotoxins are, by definition, secreted protein toxins - not structural cell-wall/membrane components and not made of lipids or polysaccharides (that describes endotoxin).

questions.stem: Which of the following inclusion bodies in the bacterial cytoplasm is INCORRECTLY described?
questions.answerRationale: Gas vesicles ("air bubbles") are enclosed by a rigid protein shell, not a lipid membrane, so calling them "membrane-bound" is the incorrect description among these inclusion bodies.

questions.stem: Which of these bacterial particles is made of two ribosome particles?
questions.answerRationale: The bacterial 70S ribosome is literally assembled from two subunits, the 30S and the 50S.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures found in some bacteria are membrane-bound organelles?

options.text: The fat droplets of G(+) bacteria.
The nucleoid of the G(-) bacteria.
Chlorosomes of the green photosynthetic bacteria.

questions.answerRationale: Magnetosomes are genuinely enclosed by a lipid membrane, making them true membrane-bound organelles - unlike the nucleoid (never membrane-bound, the defining trait of prokaryotes) or chlorosomes (enclosed by a protein monolayer, not a true membrane).

questions.stem: Which of these is a bacterial endospore?

options.text: It is a dormant cell, and its purpose is bacterial reproduction.
It is a live cell that absorbs nutrients and divides by binary fission.
It is a dormant cell, and its purpose is not reproduction, but to survive in a severely inclement environment.
It is a dormant cell that does not absorb nutrients; it does not divide, but it germinates to create a bacterium.

questions.answerRationale: An endospore is a dormant cell whose purpose is survival through a harsh environment, not reproduction - one vegetative cell forms exactly one endospore, so cell number never increases.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about the bacterial nucleoid is CORRECT?

options.text: All bacteria and their spores have a nucleoid.
The nucleoid contains chromosomes made of dsDNA.
DNA replication and RNA transcription occur in the nucleoid.
The length of bacterial genomic DNA is shorter than the length of the bacterial nucleoid.

questions.answerRationale: Because bacteria lack a nuclear envelope, both DNA replication and RNA transcription occur directly within the nucleoid region - a distinctive fact worth testing beyond the more basic observation that the nucleoid simply contains dsDNA.

questions.stem: Which of the following terms describes a bacterial shape that is very thin, long, and with many curvatures?
questions.answerRationale: Spirochetes are classically described as very thin, long, and flexible with many helical turns/curvatures - distinct from the rigid, fewer-curved spirillum.

questions.stem: An inexperienced microscopist may get confused when he observes _______ side by side.

options.text: diplococci and streptobacilli Eukaryotic cell structure

questions.answerRationale: Cocci and coccobacilli look very similar under the microscope (short rods can easily be mistaken for spheres), a classic source of confusion for beginners.

questions.stem: Challenge question: The diameter of a spherical bacterial cell is 2.0 micrometers, and that of a eukaryotic cell is 20 micrometers. How many of the bacterial cells will fit inside the eukaryotic cell (assuming that the eukaryotic cell is empty)? Note: Calculate the volume of the two cells using the formula V=4/3pr3, where p=3.14, and r is the radius (i.e., half the diameter) of the sphere.
questions.answerRationale: Volume scales with the cube of the radius: (10 µm / 1 µm)^3 = 1000, so about 1,000 of the smaller bacterial cells fit by volume inside the larger eukaryotic cell.

questions.stem: In what ways are the bacterial flagella and eukaryotic flagella similar?

options.text: The energy source used in moving the flagella.
The way the flagella are anchored to the cell.
The protein components of the filaments.

questions.answerRationale: Bacterial and eukaryotic flagella are built from completely different proteins and powered by completely different energy sources (proton motive force vs. ATP) - the one thing they genuinely share is their function, providing motility.

questions.stem: The epithelial cells of the trachea and bronchi of the lung have cilia. How the cells use the cilia.

options.text: To physically move from one location to another.
To remove mucous, debris, and microbes.
To kill microbes by sweeping actions.

questions.answerRationale: The cilia lining the trachea and bronchi drive the mucociliary escalator, sweeping mucus, trapped debris, and microbes up and out of the airway.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the cell wall of the eukaryotic cell is CORRECT?

options.text: It may contain several types of polysaccharides, proteins, silicates, carbonates, etc.
It contains short polypeptides crosslinking the polysaccharide chains.
It is buried under the plasma membrane.

questions.answerRationale: Eukaryotic cell walls are chemically diverse across lineages - polysaccharides, proteins, silicates (diatoms), carbonates, and more - unlike the uniform peptidoglycan-plus-crosslinking-peptide structure of a bacterial wall, and the wall sits outside, not under, the plasma membrane.

questions.stem: You have a fungal cell and an algal cell. How can you distinguish them if the algal cell lacks chloroplasts (i.e., the algal cell is not green)?

options.text: By the size of the cells.
By the type of polysaccharides in the cell wall.
By the presence or absence of the nucleus in the cell.
By the presence or absence of proteins in the plasma membrane.

questions.answerRationale: Without chloroplasts to use as a visual cue, fungal (chitin) and algal (cellulose) cell walls are distinguished by their different polysaccharide chemistry, since both are eukaryotic (both have a nucleus) and cell size is unreliable.

questions.stem: Challenge question: The cytoplasm of all cells has 0.9% slat. You placed these cells in fresh water from a river containing 0.05% salt. Which of the cells will burst in fresh water?

options.text: A red blood cell (erythrocyte) of a person.

questions.answerRationale: Cells with rigid walls (fungal, algal, bacterial) resist bursting in a hypotonic solution despite water influx; a red blood cell has no cell wall at all, so unchecked osmotic swelling in fresh water causes it to lyse.

questions.stem: Eukaryotic cells have three categories of the cytoskeleton. Of them, microfilaments are made of many units of the proteins named ___________, the intermediate filaments are made of many units of proteins such as ________.

options.text: alpha and beta tubulin/ alpha and beta actin
alpha and beta actin/ keratin and vimentin
keratin and vimentin/ lamins and neurofilament

questions.answerRationale: Microfilaments are built from alpha and beta actin, and intermediate filaments from proteins like keratin and vimentin - not tubulin, which instead makes up microtubules.

questions.stem: Which of these is the main function of the eukaryotic cytoskeletal proteins known as microfilaments?

options.text: Moving large organelles within the cell and chromosomes during cell division.
Moving small molecules and cytoplasm within the cell.
Maintaining the shape of the cell.

questions.answerRationale: Actin-based microfilaments drive cytoplasmic streaming and the movement of small molecules and cytoplasm within the cell; moving large organelles and chromosomes is a microtubule job.

questions.stem: Which of the following membrane phenomena is INCORRECTLY paired with a function?

options.text: Central vacuole: Storage and waste disposal.

questions.answerRationale: Lipid synthesis is the job of the smooth ER, not the rough ER, whose defining feature (ribosome-studded) is protein synthesis and processing.

questions.stem: A macrophage (a white blood cell) caught a bacterium, packed it into a membrane vesicle created from the plasma membrane, and brought it inside the cell. This process, known as phagocytosis, is a form of ________.

options.text: pinocytosis Eukaryotic cell: The Nucleus and the genome

questions.answerRationale: Phagocytosis - engulfing a particle like a bacterium into a membrane-bound vesicle - is a specific form of endocytosis (bringing material into the cell).

questions.stem: Which of these statements is INCORRECT about the nucleus of the eukaryotic cells?

options.text: The nuclear membrane has many pores for protein and RNA transport.
Chromosomes replicate, and all RNAs are transcribed in the nucleus.
The nuclear membrane is made of four layers of lipids.
A nucleus is found in eukaryotic cells all the time.

questions.answerRationale: The nucleus is not present in every eukaryotic cell "all the time" - mature mammalian red blood cells are enucleated, and the nuclear envelope itself breaks down during mitosis in many cell types.

questions.stem: Which of these DNA molecules in a cell can be called chromatin?

options.text: Two DNA molecules, highly folded (condensed) and tied together by the proteins named cohesins.
DNA bound to histone proteins forming nucleosomes and 11 nm and/or 30 nm fibers.
Folded DNA, found in bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic cells.
Small DNA molecules in the cytoplasm of some cells.

questions.answerRationale: Chromatin is, by definition, DNA wound around histone proteins to form nucleosomes and the higher-order 11 nm and 30 nm fibers - not simply any folded DNA, and not sister chromatids joined by cohesins.

questions.stem: Challenge question: Why are mitochondria and chloroplasts called (endosymbiotic) bacteria?

options.text: They live inside eukaryotic cells; they cannot survive outside the host cell.
They have DNA, RNA, proteins, ribosomes, and they can synthesize ATP.
They have genomes made of short, circular dsDNA molecules.
They have an endoplasmic membrane like eukaryotic cells.

questions.answerRationale: A short, circular dsDNA genome is the hallmark bacterial genome architecture, and finding exactly that inside mitochondria and chloroplasts is the strongest structural evidence tying them to a bacterial (endosymbiotic) origin.

questions.stem: Which of these is a mitochondrion (and not a chloroplast)?

options.text: It most likely evolved from aerobic bacteria.
It has pigments like chlorophyll in its membrane.
It most likely evolved from photosynthetic bacteria.

questions.answerRationale: Mitochondria most likely evolved from an aerobic bacterium capable of oxidative phosphorylation, while chloroplasts evolved from a photosynthetic bacterium (cyanobacterium) - both organelles can make ATP, so that alone doesn't distinguish them.

questions.stem: Which of these, according to the endosymbiosis theory on the evolution of eukaryotic cells, is the last of the events?

options.text: The nucleoid of the ancestral eukaryotic cell received a membrane envelope.
The ancestral eukaryotic cell grew larger and needed to develop endoplasmic membranes.
A photosynthetic bacterium entered the ancestral eukaryotic cells that already had an endosymbiont.
An aerobic bacterium (capable of using oxygen for ATP synthesis) invaded the ancestral eukaryotic cell.

questions.answerRationale: Because mitochondria are found in essentially all eukaryotes while chloroplasts are limited to photosynthetic lineages, the aerobic bacterium (future mitochondrion) must have been acquired first; the photosynthetic bacterium (future chloroplast) entered a cell that already had that endosymbiont, making it the last event.

questions.stem: Why can the bacteria of the genus Wolbachia found in the cells of the nematode Wuchereria sp. be called an eukaryotic organelle?

options.text: If the bacterium is selectively killed, the host cell fails to grow or dies.
It provides some nutrients essential for the host cell.
The bacterium cannot survive outside the host cell.
The bacterium lives inside the eukaryotic cell.

questions.answerRationale: Wolbachia in Wuchereria satisfies every one of these organelle-like criteria simultaneously - obligate for host survival, nutrient-providing, unable to survive outside the host, and permanently intracellular - which together, not any single trait alone, is what justifies calling it an organelle.

questions.stem: How and why do you fix bacterial cells for light microscopic examination?

options.text: How: Make a smear on a slide, air-dry, then briefly flame; why: to prevent the cells from being washed away during staining.
How: Make a smear on a slide using formaldehyde and air-dry; why: To make sure the shape of the cell remains intact during staining.

questions.answerRationale: The standard heat-fixation method - smear, air-dry, briefly pass through a flame - adheres cells to the slide so they aren't washed away during the staining steps that follow.

questions.stem: A lab technician is processing a small piece of liver for microscopic examination. Which is the third step of processing?

options.text: Embed the sample in wax or epoxy.
Put the sample in a formaldehyde solution.
Cut the sample into thin slices using a microtome.

questions.answerRationale: Standard tissue processing runs: fix in formaldehyde, dehydrate, embed in wax or epoxy, then section with a microtome - making embedding the third step.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is CORRECT about common dyes/pigments used in staining bacteria?

options.text: The chromophore of crystal violet is negatively charged and cannot bind cellular components.
The chromophore of safranin is positively charged and binds certain cellular components.
Eosin is a basic dye, and it binds to some cellular components.
Carbol fuschin is a neutral dye.

questions.answerRationale: Safranin's chromophore is positively charged and binds negatively charged cellular components - crystal violet is likewise positively charged (not negative), eosin is an acidic (not basic) dye, carbol fuchsin is a basic (not neutral) dye, and Giemsa is a mixed acidic/basic dye, not purely acidic.

questions.stem: Challenge question: A laboratory technician is conducting Gram staining of a pathological sample containing a mixture of bacterial species. She fixed the sample on a glass slide, stained it with crystal violet, rinsed, then soaked it in iodine solution, and then washed it with dilute alcohol. She forgot to counterstain the slide and went on to examine it under a light microscope. Which of the following bacteria can she see on the slide?

options.text: Treponema pallidum, a very thin spirochete.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a bacterium lacking a cell wall.

questions.answerRationale: Without the safranin counterstain, only Gram-positive bacteria - which retain the crystal violet-iodine complex through decolorization - remain visible; Gram-negative bacteria are decolorized and invisible without the pink counterstain, and Mycoplasma and the very thin Treponema aren't reliably seen this way regardless.

questions.stem: Which of these two staining methods requires the sample to be heated over a flame for five minutes?

options.text: Acid-fast staining and Schaffer-Fulton endospore staining.
Schaffer-Fulton endospore staining and Leifson flagella staining.
Leifson flagella staining and negative staining of bacterial capsule using India ink.
Negative staining of bacterial capsule using India ink and simple staining with safranin.

questions.answerRationale: Both acid-fast staining and the Schaffer-Fulton endospore stain require heating (steaming) the specimen for several minutes to drive the primary stain through, respectively, the waxy mycolic acid coat or the tough endospore coat; Leifson flagella stain and India ink capsule stain are both done at room temperature.

questions.stem: Which of the following eukaryotic microbe samples (all wet-mounted on a glass slide) is unsuitable for examination using a simple LM?

options.text: Protozoa- fixed and stained with hematoxylin.

questions.answerRationale: Calcofluor white is a fluorochrome that only becomes visible under a fluorescence/UV microscope - it is useless on a simple brightfield LM, unlike the other unstained or conventionally-stained wet mounts listed.

questions.stem: Why are light microscopes (LMs) not used in examining virus particles?

options.text: Viruses are too tiny; LMs cannot resolve them.
Viruses cannot be stained with acidic, basic, or fluorescent dyes.
Viruses are soluble in water; they cannot be harvested for microscopic examination.

questions.answerRationale: Virus particles (roughly 20-300 nm) fall well below the ~200 nm resolution limit of light microscopy, so LMs simply cannot resolve them as distinct structures - not a staining or cellularity issue.

questions.stem: Which of these can NOT be directly used in phylogenetic classification of organisms?

options.text: The nucleotide sequence of one gene (i.e., the 16s RNA gene) of organisms.
The nucleotide sequence of the whole genome of the genome creatures.
The structure and physiologic abilities of organisms.

questions.answerRationale: Phylogenetic classification is based on genetic/molecular sequence data (a single gene or a whole genome); structure and physiology are phenotypic traits used in the older, separate approach of phenetic classification.

questions.stem: Which of these microbes is a primary pathogen?

options.text: It is found in both healthy and sick people.
It causes disease in some individuals but not in others.
It can be found in the environments and healthy humans.
It can cause disease only in individuals with a compromised immune system.

questions.answerRationale: A primary (frank) pathogen is defined by its ability to cause disease in otherwise healthy, immunocompetent hosts - unlike opportunists, which only cause disease under compromised conditions.

questions.stem: Which of these is a nucleocapsid?

options.text: It has capsomeres directly bound to the genome.
It serves as a container to house a genome.
It is made of many capsomeres.

questions.answerRationale: A nucleocapsid is, by general definition, the protein shell that serves as a container housing the viral genome - "made of many capsomeres" or "icosahedral" describe only specific capsid shapes, not the general nucleocapsid concept.

questions.stem: Which of these genome structures does not make a class in the Baltimore classification of viruses?
questions.answerRationale: The seven Baltimore classes are defined by genome chemistry - strandedness, polarity, and replication strategy (dsDNA, ssDNA, dsRNA, +ssRNA, -ssRNA, and the two reverse-transcribing classes) - not by whether the genome happens to be circular or linear.

questions.stem: Which of the viral genome types is considered equivalent to mRNA?
questions.answerRationale: A (+)ssRNA genome can be translated directly by host ribosomes exactly like an mRNA molecule, which is literally how Baltimore Class IV is defined.

questions.stem: Which of these herpes viruses may cause shingles?
questions.answerRationale: Shingles is caused by reactivation of the same virus that causes chickenpox: HSV-3, the varicella-zoster virus.

questions.stem: All these viruses can cause cancers in human beings. Which of them is a member of Poxviridae?
questions.answerRationale: Molluscum contagiosum virus is the cancer-associated virus classified in family Poxviridae; the others belong to Adenoviridae, Herpesviridae (x2), and Papillomaviridae.

questions.stem: The only major pathogenic virus with a ssDNA genome is ________, and the only major pathogenic virus with a dsRNA genome is ___________, repectively.
questions.answerRationale: Human parvovirus is the classic pathogenic ssDNA virus, and rotavirus is the classic pathogenic dsRNA virus.

questions.stem: There are six viruses with the word “hepatitis” in their common name. Which of them is the dsDNA retrovirus?
questions.answerRationale: Hepatitis B virus is uniquely a dsDNA virus that replicates through a reverse-transcriptase step, unlike the other hepatitis viruses, which are all RNA viruses.

questions.stem: Which of these is a coronavirus (Family Coronaviridae)?
questions.answerRationale: MERS-CoV is a coronavirus (family Coronaviridae); SLEV, WNEV, and WEEV are all encephalitis-causing flaviviruses/alphaviruses, not coronaviruses.

questions.stem: All these viruses cause hemorrhagic fevers, EXCEPT __________, it causes skin rashes, fever and arthritis.
questions.answerRationale: Chikungunya virus causes fever, joint pain (arthritis), and rash rather than hemorrhagic fever, unlike Ebola, Hantavirus, Pumala virus, and Marburg virus.

questions.stem: All these viruses cause respiratory syndromes. Which of them causes giant cell (i.e., fused cell) pneumonia among children?
questions.answerRationale: Respiratory syncytial virus is literally named for causing syncytia - fused giant cells - in pediatric pneumonia.

questions.stem: All these viruses cause encephalitis (inflammation of the brain cells). Which of them is buniyavirus (family Peribuniyaviride)?
questions.answerRationale: California encephalitis virus belongs to genus Orthobunyavirus within family Peribunyaviridae; the others are an arenavirus and an alphavirus.

questions.stem: Which of these viruses is an ssRNA retrovirus?
questions.answerRationale: HTLV-1 (Human T-lymphotropic virus 1) is a classic ssRNA retrovirus; the others are flaviviruses or a dsDNA-RT hepadnavirus.

questions.stem: Which of this information about plant viruses is INCORRECT?

options.text: Some plant viruses infect animals such as insects.
Plant viruses can have a twin-icosahedral capsid.
Biologically active plant viruses can be isolated from the feces of healthy people.
The estimated annual cost of plant virus damage to crop production is about 100 billion.
Gardeners may unknowingly transmit plant viruses from infected plants to healthy plants.

questions.answerRationale: Commonly cited estimates put global crop losses from plant viruses closer to tens of billions of dollars annually, not $100 billion - the other statements about insect-infecting plant viruses, twin-icosahedral capsids, viable virus in healthy feces, and gardener transmission are all documented facts.

questions.stem: The steps of the lytic replication cycle of bacterial viruses are shown. Which of them is step 4 from the beginning?

options.text: Infection of a new host cell by a virus.
Release of newly generated virus particles from the damaged host cell.

questions.answerRationale: The lytic cycle runs: infection, genome replication, protein synthesis, production of progeny particles (assembly), then release - making assembly of progeny particles the fourth step.

questions.stem: Why is a bacteriophage with a lysogenic replication cycle not suitable for phage therapy? Note: A lysogen is a bacterium that has a genome of a bacteriophage integrated in its chromosome.

options.text: It protects the lysogens from reinfection by the bacteriophages.
It inactivates bacteriophages with a lytic replication cycle.
It makes the lysogen replicate more rapidly.

questions.answerRationale: Lysogeny confers immunity to reinfection (superinfection exclusion) on the bacterial host, meaning the target bacteria become resistant to further phage killing - defeating the purpose of phage therapy.

questions.stem: All these bacterial phyla that have pathogenic species. Which of them only have G(+) cells?
questions.answerRationale: Actinobacteria (high-GC Gram-positive bacteria like Mycobacterium and Corynebacterium) are essentially uniformly Gram-positive, without the Gram-negative-like exceptions found within Firmicutes.

questions.stem: Which of these aerobic G(+) cocci is a primary pathogen?
questions.answerRationale: Streptococcus pyogenes is a classic primary pathogen, causing disease like strep throat and necrotizing fasciitis in healthy people, unlike the other options, which are normal-flora/opportunistic species.

questions.stem: All these are Actinobacteria with mycolic acid in their cell wall. Which of them causes opportunistic tuberculosis-like diseases among immunocompromised subjects?
questions.answerRationale: Mycobacterium intracellulare (part of the Mycobacterium avium complex) is the textbook cause of opportunistic, TB-like disease in immunocompromised patients, especially those with AIDS.

questions.stem: Which of these aerobic G(+) bacterial species is infamous for causing bacteremia from contaminated food?
questions.answerRationale: Listeria monocytogenes is THE classic foodborne bacteremia/sepsis pathogen, associated with contaminated deli meats, soft cheeses, and unpasteurized dairy.

questions.stem: Which of these aerobic G(_) coccus is also known a gonococcus?
questions.answerRationale: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the organism commonly called the gonococcus.

questions.stem: Of these members of the Enterobacteriaceae, _______________ causes severe pneumonia and ________ causes plague.
questions.answerRationale: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a well-known cause of severe pneumonia, and Yersinia pestis causes plague - both members of Enterobacteriaceae.

questions.stem: All these are flagellated G(-) bacilli. Which of them is associated with stomach cancer?
questions.answerRationale: Helicobacter pylori is the well-established cause of gastric cancer and peptic ulcer disease among these flagellated Gram-negative bacilli.

questions.stem: Which of these G(-) rods causes whooping cough?
questions.answerRationale: Bordetella pertussis causes whooping cough (pertussis).

questions.stem: Which of these anaerobic G(+) rods causes severe but only opportunistic intestinal infections?
questions.answerRationale: Clostridioides difficile is the textbook example of an opportunistic intestinal pathogen, causing severe pseudomembranous colitis specifically after normal gut flora is disrupted, usually by antibiotics.

questions.stem: Which of these anaerobic G(-) rod-shaped bacterial species has a spindle-shaped cell? Note: It causes surgical wound infection and gum infections.
questions.answerRationale: Fusobacterium literally means "spindle-shaped," and F. nucleatum is associated with surgical wound and gum infections.

questions.stem: Which of these spirochaete causes Lyme disease?
questions.answerRationale: Borrelia burgdorferi is the spirochete that causes Lyme disease.

questions.stem: All these pathogenic bacteria are unusual (some lack the cell wall, and some only replicate by sporulating). Which of them cause a very common sexually transmitted infection?
questions.answerRationale: Chlamydia trachomatis causes the most common bacterial sexually transmitted infection.

questions.stem: The only algal genus that has genuine animal pathogens is Prototheca. Which of this information about this genus is CORRECT?

options.text: It causes lung infections among humans.
It lacks cellulose in its cell wall.

questions.answerRationale: Prototheca reproduces asexually by internal septation, producing multiple autospores within a sporangium - a process reasonably described as sporulation; its defining trait is actually the LACK of chloroplasts, not their presence.

questions.stem: Which of this information about harmful algal bloom (HAB) is CORRECT?

options.text: It is triggered by stresses such as a lack of nutrients and unseasonal cold weather.
It can be triggered by the overgrowth of some algae or cyanobacteria.
It increases dissolved oxygen in water, leading to fish death.
It occurs only in coastal seawater.

questions.answerRationale: A harmful algal bloom is, by definition, an overgrowth of algae or cyanobacteria - typically triggered by excess nutrients and warm conditions, and it depletes rather than increases dissolved oxygen, killing fish through hypoxia; it also occurs in freshwater, not only coastal seawater.

questions.stem: All these are algal toxins produced by certain species of algae during HAB or other stressful situations, EXCEPT _________, which are fungal toxins.
questions.answerRationale: Aflatoxin and citrinin are fungal mycotoxins; pectenotoxins, pfiesteria toxins, brevetoxin, dinophysis toxins, gonyautoxin, and okadaic acid are all algal toxins.

questions.stem: How do people get paralytic shellfish poisoning? Note: HAB- harmful algal bloom.

options.text: They swim or wade into water affected with HAB.
They eat fish caught from water affected with HAB.
They eat shellfish harvested from water affected with HAB.
They live close to coasts affected by HAB and inhale air contaminated with algal toxins.

questions.answerRationale: Filter-feeding shellfish (mussels, clams, oysters) bioaccumulate the causative toxin (saxitoxin) from HAB-affected water, and eating them is how people develop paralytic shellfish poisoning.

questions.stem: Many pathogenic fungi are dimorphic. Which of these structures can a dimorphic fungus have?
questions.answerRationale: "Dimorphic" means a fungus can exist in two forms - typically a yeast form at body temperature/in tissue and a mold form in the environment - as seen in Histoplasma, Blastomyces, and Coccidioides.

questions.stem: Some fungi produce toxins such as aflatoxins, ochratoxins, citrinins, fumonisins, trichothecenes, and ergot toxins. Which of these is NOT a significant source of the mycotoxins for human exposure? Note: Assume that the USDA had not inspected the items.

options.text: Fruits, fruit juice, pork, and beef.
Peanuts, peanut butter, and oils extracted from affected crops.

questions.answerRationale: Cultivated edible mushrooms and truffles are not a significant mycotoxin source for humans; mycotoxins instead come from molds contaminating cereals, nuts, fruit, and animal feed.

questions.stem: Which of these properties describes the fungal group Zygomycota?

options.text: Spores produced after sexual reproduction are found in a ball-shaped sporangium.
Spores produced after sexual reproduction are found in a tubular basidium.
Spores produced after sexual reproduction are found in a tubular ascus.
The group does not produce sexually and produces no sexual spores.

questions.answerRationale: Zygomycota is named for the thick-walled zygospore it produces during sexual reproduction, formed within a ball-shaped zygosporangium.

questions.stem: Which of these Zygomycota fungi can be considered a primary pathogen?
questions.answerRationale: Basidiobolus ranarum causes chronic subcutaneous zygomycosis in otherwise healthy (immunocompetent) people, especially in the tropics, unlike Mucor species, which are classic opportunists restricted to immunocompromised hosts.

questions.stem: Which of these Ascomycota fungi cause opportunistic lung mycoses and also produce mycotoxins such as aflatoxins?
questions.answerRationale: Aspergillus fumigatus causes opportunistic lung mycoses (aspergillosis) and belongs to a genus well known for producing mycotoxins like aflatoxin.

questions.stem: All these fungi are primary pathogens that cause skin or lung mycoses. Which of them also causes valley fever?
questions.answerRationale: Coccidioides immitis causes coccidioidomycosis, popularly known as Valley Fever.

questions.stem: None of these fungi can be considered a primary pathogen. Which of them causes thrush and the most reported fungal infections in the Western Hemisphere?
questions.answerRationale: Candida albicans causes oral thrush and is responsible for the most commonly reported fungal infections in the Western Hemisphere.

questions.stem: Organisms of which of these protozoan phyla move using pseudopodia?
questions.answerRationale: Sarcodina (the amoebae) are defined by moving via pseudopodia.

questions.stem: Which of these is CORRECT about protozoan cysts?

options.text: Cysts have a thick polysaccharide cell wall.
Cysts are more vulnerable to extreme environmental factors than trophozoites.

questions.answerRationale: A protozoan cyst's defining feature is a thick, protective polysaccharide cell wall - cysts are dormant and metabolically reduced (not actively absorbing nutrients or dividing) and are specifically the environmentally RESISTANT stage, not the more vulnerable one.

questions.stem: Which of these mastigophore protozoans causes African sleeping sickness?
questions.answerRationale: Trypanosoma brucei, a flagellate (mastigophoran) protozoan, causes African sleeping sickness.

questions.stem: Which of these amoebae causes opportunistic eye and brain infections among unscrupulous contact lens users?
questions.answerRationale: Acanthamoeba castellanii is classically linked to contact-lens-associated keratitis and can also cause granulomatous brain infection.

questions.stem: Which of these apicomplexan protozoa causes malaria?
