questions.answerRationale: Plasmodium falciparum, an apicomplexan protozoan, causes malaria.

questions.stem: Only one ciliate protozoan causes significant human disease in the United States. Which of these is the ciliate?
questions.answerRationale: Balantidium coli is the only ciliate protozoan that causes significant human disease in the United States.

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics is specific to trematodes but not all flatworms?
questions.answerRationale: A syncytial tegument (a multinucleate covering with no individual cell membranes) is shared by the parasitic flatworms - trematodes and cestodes - but not by free-living, ciliated turbellarian flatworms, so it is not a trait of "all flatworms."

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a route for flatworm infections in humans?

options.text: Getting bitten by Culex or Aedes mosquitoes.

questions.answerRationale: Mosquitoes (Culex, Aedes) transmit roundworms like filarial worms, not flatworms/trematodes, which instead spread through undercooked fish, crustaceans, contaminated water vegetables, or skin penetration while wading.

questions.stem: Which of these flukes is associated with human cancers, especially prostate cancer?
questions.answerRationale: Schistosoma haematobium's urogenital tropism, beyond its well-established link to bladder cancer, extends to pelvic organs including the prostate.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic that cestodes share with trematodes? Note: both cestodes and trematodes are flatworms.
questions.answerRationale: Both cestodes (via the scolex) and trematodes have suckers as attachment organs - cestodes alone are segmented with proglottids and lack a gut, while trematodes retain a simple blind intestine.

questions.stem: Cysticercosis is a disease characterized by the growth of worm larvae in the skin, internal organs, and the brain of the infected subject. Which of these cestodes (tapeworms) may cause cysticercosis?
questions.answerRationale: Taenia solium, the pork tapeworm, causes cysticercosis when its larvae migrate into skin, organs, or the brain.

questions.stem: Hydatid cysts are spaces within solid organs where trematode worm larvae grow and reproduce asexually. Which of these tapeworms may cause hydatid cysts?
questions.answerRationale: Echinococcus multilocularis causes hydatid (alveolar hydatid) cyst disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following characteristics is unique for nematode worms (compared to other worms including earthworms)?
questions.answerRationale: A pseudocoelom (a body cavity not fully lined by mesoderm) is the textbook defining feature that separates nematodes from acoelomate flatworms and from true-coelomate annelids like earthworms.

questions.stem: Which of these may expose a person to roundworm infection?

options.text: Walking barefoot on the lawn and in parks.

questions.answerRationale: Contaminated produce, barefoot contact with soil, undercooked meat/fish, and mosquito bites are all real transmission routes for different specific roundworm species.

questions.stem: About 1.2 billion people have ascariasis (are currently infected with Ascaris lumbricoides). Which of the following is the deadliest outcome of ascariasis?
questions.answerRationale: A heavy Ascaris burden can form a mass that completely obstructs the intestine, the most commonly cited severe, potentially fatal complication of ascariasis.

questions.stem: Which of these roundworm infections is manifested by irritations in the rectum and anus (specially among children)?
questions.answerRationale: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) causes the classic perianal itching, especially in children, as females migrate to the anus at night to lay eggs.

questions.stem: Hookworms are tiny, but they bite into the intestine and suck blood. Which of these worms is NOT a hookworm?
questions.answerRationale: Dracunculus medinensis (Guinea worm) is transmitted via contaminated water containing infected copepods, an entirely different biology from the soil-transmitted, skin-penetrating true hookworms Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus.

questions.stem: All these roundworms are transmitted to humans by mosquitoes or flies. Which of them causes African river blindness?
questions.answerRationale: Onchocerca volvulus causes onchocerciasis, popularly known as African river blindness.

questions.stem: All these roundworms are transmitted to humans by mosquitoes or flies. Which of them may cause blockage of lymphatic vessels, causing elephantiasis?
questions.answerRationale: Brugia malayi and Wuchereria bancrofti are the lymphatic filariasis worms that block lymphatic vessels and cause elephantiasis.

questions.stem: Which of these invertebrates can cause a lasting parasitic infection in a human subject?
questions.answerRationale: Linguatula serrata, an unusual pentastomid arthropod, can cause a lasting visceral infection (pentastomiasis) as its larvae persist in internal organs - unlike a leech's temporary feeding or the venomous, non-parasitic bites/stings of the others.

questions.stem: Which of the following arthropod vectors is paired with an infectious disease that it does not transmit?
questions.answerRationale: The tsetse fly transmits African sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis), not river blindness - river blindness (onchocerciasis) is instead transmitted by blackflies, making this the mismatched pair.

questions.stem: Which of these arthropods may cause myiasis (maggot in human wounds)?
questions.answerRationale: Dermatobia hominis, the human botfly, is the classic myiasis-causing organism, with larvae that burrow directly into skin.

chapters.title: Microbial Metabolism I: Catabolic Reactions for ATP Synthesis

questions.stem: Energy is produced in the cell through ________ reactions, consumed by _______ reactions; and together they are ________ reactions.
questions.answerRationale: Catabolic reactions release energy, anabolic reactions consume it; together both are called metabolic reactions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a catabolic reaction?

options.text: Producing sugar from CO2 and water.

questions.answerRationale: Breaking down amino acids to release energy for ATP synthesis is catabolic; the other three all build larger molecules (anabolic).

questions.stem: Which of these is an anabolic reaction?

options.text: Removing an amine group from an amino acid.
Removing an electron from an organic acid.

questions.answerRationale: Synthesizing proteins from amino acids builds a larger molecule from smaller ones - anabolic. The others break bonds (catabolic).

questions.stem: Which of these is a covalent bond?

options.text: It is created by an anion and a cation.
It is formed by two atoms sharing an electron.
It is formed by two atoms sharing a pair of electrons.
It is created between two atoms placed within 0.5 nm, and the atoms have positive and negative induction on opposite sides.
It is formed because of the electrostatic attraction of delta-positive and delta-negative induction of two covalent compounds, one with a hydrogen atom.

questions.answerRationale: A covalent bond is defined by two atoms SHARING A PAIR of electrons. (B) is wrong because covalent bonds share a pair, not a single electron; (D)/(E) describe weaker non-covalent interactions.

questions.stem: Which of these bonds is most likely a hydrogen bond?
questions.answerRationale: Hydrogen bonds are weak, roughly ~1-5 kcal/mol - far weaker than a covalent bond (tens of kcal/mol). 1.9 kcal/mol is the realistic order of magnitude among the choices.

questions.stem: Which of these is a high-energy compound?

options.text: It has one or more unstable covalent bonds.
It has one or more stable covalent bonds.
It is made of unstable ionic bonds.

questions.answerRationale: A high-energy compound has one or more UNSTABLE covalent bonds that release a large amount of energy when broken (e.g. the phosphoanhydride bonds in ATP).

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of the following chemical compounds can be considered a high-energy compound?
questions.answerRationale: Pyrophosphate (PO3-O-PO3) has the unstable phosphoanhydride bond - the same type of high-energy bond found in ATP. Water and CO2 are fully stable/oxidized; ethylene’s double bond is not a "high-energy" biochemical bond in this sense.

sections.heading: Inorganic compounds of the cell and water effects

questions.stem: How does CO2 exist in the cell?
questions.answerRationale: At physiological (near-neutral) pH, dissolved CO2 mostly exists as bicarbonate ion (HCO3-) after hydrating to carbonic acid and dissociating.

questions.stem: Why do inorganic compounds and polar organic compounds readily interact with water?

options.text: Water is a polar covalent compound.
Water is a non-polar covalent compound.
Inorganic compounds and polar organic compounds are hydrophobic.

questions.answerRationale: Water is a polar covalent molecule, so it hydrogen-bonds/interacts readily with other polar or charged (inorganic) compounds.

questions.stem: You mixed some octane (i.e., petroleum) with water, shook the mixture, and then allowed it to settle. The octane molecules accumulated on the water's surface. Which of the interactions must have NOT occurred in the glass?

options.text: Octane molecules and water molecules formed some ionic bonds.
Water molecules interact with each other and form many hydrogen bonds.
Water molecules excluded octane molecules from the spaces between water molecules.
Octane molecules interacted with one another, forming many van der Waals interactions.

questions.answerRationale: Octane (a nonpolar hydrocarbon) cannot form ionic bonds with water at all - that interaction never happens. The other three interactions (water-water H-bonds, water excluding octane, octane-octane van der Waals) are exactly what causes the separation.

questions.stem: You placed an E. coli cell (its cytoplasm has 1% salt) in a glass of pure water (has less than 0.1% salt). Which of these would happen?

options.text: Water from the glass will move into the cell, causing it to burst.
Cytoplasmic water will move out to the glass, causing the cell to shrink.
Water from the glass will move into the cell, but will not cause the cell to burst.
Salt from the cytoplasm will migrate out of the cell to the glass, causing the cell to shrink.

questions.answerRationale: The cell is hypertonic to the surrounding pure water, so water moves IN by osmosis - but bacteria have a rigid cell wall that resists the resulting turgor pressure, so the cell does not burst.

questions.stem: All these were dissolved in water. Which of these is an acid?
questions.answerRationale: Acetic acid dissociates to release H+ (a proton) - the defining behavior of an acid. (B) releases OH- (a base); (C) is a neutral salt; (D) does not dissociate at all.

questions.stem: Which of these body fluids has the lowest concentration of protons (H+) or hydronium ions (H3O+)?
questions.answerRationale: Lowest [H+] = highest pH. Blood at pH 7.4 is the highest pH listed, so it has the fewest protons/hydronium ions.

questions.stem: Functional groups replace H atoms in a hydrocarbon to form new organic compounds. Which of these functional groups is the carboxylic acid group?
questions.answerRationale: COOH is the carboxylic acid functional group by definition.

questions.stem: Which of these lipid molecules is amphipathic for having a lipid tail and a hydrophilic head group?
questions.answerRationale: A phosphoglycerolipid (phospholipid) has a hydrophobic fatty-acid tail AND a hydrophilic phosphate head group - the textbook definition of amphipathic. Triglycerides and octane have no polar head group.

questions.stem: Which of the following monosaccharides has a 4-carbon skeleton?
questions.answerRationale: A tetrose has a 4-carbon skeleton; erythrose is the tetrose in the list (glycerol=3C, ribose=5C, fructose=6C, sedoheptulose=7C).

questions.stem: A glycosidic bond is a covalent bond formed between a sugar molecule and another molecule. Which of the following molecules lacks a glycosidic bond?
questions.answerRationale: Free glucose by itself has no glycosidic bond (nothing is attached to it yet) - unlike maltose (paired with it here), which does have one, and unlike every item in the other three options, which all genuinely have a glycosidic-type linkage.

questions.stem: Which of the following would distinguish an amino acid from a fatty acid or an organic acid?
questions.answerRationale: The -NH2 (amino) group is what makes an amino acid an amino acid - fatty acids and other organic acids have a -COOH group but no amino group.

questions.stem: Of the 20 alpha amino caids, _________ has three NH2 groups and _______ has two carboxylic acid groups.
questions.answerRationale: Arginine’s guanidino side chain effectively carries three nitrogen/amine-type groups; aspartic acid has two carboxylic acid groups (the alpha-COOH plus a side-chain COOH).

questions.stem: Which of these atoms are found in the R group of all polar and charged amino acids but not in the R group of the nonpolar amino acids?
questions.answerRationale: N and O (in -OH, -COOH, -NH2, -CONH2 side chains) are what make an R group polar/charged; C and H alone are nonpolar and present in every amino acid, so they cannot be the distinguishing atoms.

questions.stem: Which of these shows a purine base and a (ribo) nucleoside, respectively?
questions.answerRationale: Adenine is a purine BASE; guanosine (guanine + ribose, no phosphate) is a ribonucleoSIDE - matching "a purine base and a ribonucleoside respectively." The other options pair a nucleoside with a nucleotide, not a base with a nucleoside.

questions.stem: Which of these distinguishes a ribonucleotide and a deoxyribonucleotide?

options.text: The type of ribose sugar used in making the nucleotides.
The type of purine nucleotides used in making the nucleotides.
The number of phosphate groups used in making the nucleotides.

questions.answerRationale: Ribonucleotides use ribose; deoxyribonucleotides use deoxyribose (missing the 2’-OH) - the sugar is the defining difference, not the base or phosphate count.

questions.stem: Which of these polysaccharides is a stored food source, not a structural component of the cell?
questions.answerRationale: Glycogen is the storage polysaccharide (in animals/bacteria). Cellulose, chitin, and murein (peptidoglycan) are all structural.

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of the following pairs of polymers share the same types of components?
questions.answerRationale: Nucleic acids (nucleotides, which include a sugar) and polysaccharides (built entirely of sugars) share sugar-based building blocks; proteins/nucleic acids and proteins/polysaccharides do not share a common monomer type.

questions.stem: Which of these nucleic acid molecules must be RNA?

options.text: It is the genome of a virus.

questions.answerRationale: The sequence contains U (uracil), which is unique to RNA - DNA never has uracil. A sequence with T is DNA, not RNA; being single-stranded or being a viral genome does not guarantee RNA (DNA can be either too).

questions.stem: Which of these statements about nucleic acids cannot be CORRECT?

options.text: An ssRNA and an ssDNA molecule can make a double-stranded molecule of nucleic acids.
An ssRNA may fold and create dsRNA stems and single-stranded RNA loops.
The genomic DNA of all cells is double-stranded.
All nucleic acid molecules have 5’ and a 3’ end.
Some viruses have a dsRNA genome.

questions.answerRationale: Circular nucleic acid molecules (plasmids, many circular viral genomes) are closed loops with no free ends at all, so they do NOT have a 5’ and 3’ end - this statement cannot be universally correct. RNA-DNA hybrids, folded ssRNA, dsDNA genomes in all cells, and dsRNA viral genomes are all real and correct.

questions.stem: The size of human chromosome 1 is 249 mbp. What is the length of it in centimeters if one bp of DNA is 0.34 nanometers?
Which of these is the secondary structure of a long polypeptide chain?

options.text: The amino acid sequence of the polypeptide chain.
The alpha helices and beta sheets, formed on the polypeptide chains.
The three-dimensional structure of a folded single polypropylene chain.
The three-dimensional structure of two polypropylene chains folded together.

questions.answerRationale: Alpha helices and beta sheets are, by definition, the SECONDARY structure of a polypeptide (sequence = primary; single folded chain = tertiary; multiple chains together = quaternary).

questions.stem: High fever (about 40 oC or 104 oF) may cause a person to have convulsions and coma. Which of these explains the condition?

options.text: High temperatures break hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces, damaging protein structure.
The high temperature breaks down peptide bonds that hold the amino acids of the proteins.
The high temperature causes the cytoplasm to boil and the cells to burst.

questions.answerRationale: High fever denatures proteins by breaking the weak hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces that hold secondary/tertiary structure - it does not break the strong covalent peptide bonds, and 40°C is nowhere near boiling.

questions.stem: A chemical reaction has a delta (D)G of -1.5 kcal/mol. Which of the following statements is correct about this reaction?

options.text: The reactants have more energy than the products.
The reactants have less energy than the products.
The reactants and products have similar energy.
The reactants are more stable than the products.

questions.answerRationale: A negative ΔG (exergonic, energy released) means the reactants started out with MORE energy than the (lower-energy, more stable) products - the opposite of options B and D, and (E) is wrong because negative ΔG is exergonic, not endergonic.

questions.stem: Which of the following chemical reactions is endergonic and will not start unless heat energy is applied?

options.text: X + Y à XY, DG= -11 kcal/mol.
P + Q à PQ, DG= -1.1 kcal/mol.

questions.answerRationale: A positive ΔG (+11 kcal/mol) means the reaction is endergonic and will not proceed spontaneously without an outside energy input (like heat). The other two have negative ΔG (exergonic, spontaneous).

questions.stem: Activation energy may be necessary for the initiation of __________ reactions, because __________.

options.text: only the endergonic reactions/ the reactants are low-energy/stable compounds
only the exergonic reactions/ the reactants are high-energy/unstable compounds
all endergonic and almost all exergonic reactions/ the reactants must move and collide Catalysis and the catalysts

questions.answerRationale: Activation energy is needed for essentially all reactions (endergonic and almost all exergonic) because reactant molecules must first collide with enough energy and the right orientation to reach the transition state - it is not limited to just one thermodynamic category.

questions.stem: Which of these statements about catalysts is CORRECT?

options.text: Catalysts are used up in the reaction process.
Catalysts do not take part in the chemical reaction.
Catalysts reduce the activation energy of chemical reactions.
Catalysts increase the activation energy of chemical reactions.

questions.answerRationale: A catalyst’s defining role is lowering the activation energy of a reaction; it is not consumed, and it does participate (transiently) in the reaction mechanism.

questions.stem: A naturally occurring cellular enzyme can be made of any of the following components EXCEPT_______.
questions.answerRationale: Naturally occurring cellular enzymes can be proteins, RNAs (ribozymes), or RNA-protein complexes (like the ribosome) - but never DNA. DNA-based catalysts (deoxyribozymes) are lab-made, not found in nature.

questions.stem: Enzymes reduce the need for the activation energy of a chemical reaction and help complete the reactions at the physiological conditions (i.e., about 20 °C, one atmosphere of pressure, and neutral pH) by each of the following methods EXCEPT by________.

options.text: placing stress and strains on the bound reactants to achieve the transition state
binding and bringing the reactants close to each other in the proper orientation
increasing pressure and temperature within the enzyme reaction site Metabolic pathways and enzyme regulation

questions.answerRationale: Enzymes work at existing physiological temperature and pressure - they lower activation energy through binding/orientation and inducing strain on the substrate, not by physically raising the temperature or pressure at the active site.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a reason for the cell to have many enzymes and many metabolic pathways?

options.text: One enzyme only catalyzes one or a few reactions.
The cell uses the product of one reaction as the reactant of another reaction.
It needs many different reactions to break or synthesize one large molecule
The cell regulates enzymes and the production and destruction of cellular molecules.
The enzymes are made of proteins, RNAs, or RNA-protein complexes; they are relatively unstable.

questions.answerRationale: That enzymes are made of proteins/RNA/RNA-protein complexes and are relatively unstable is a true fact about enzyme composition, but it does not explain WHY the cell needs MANY DIFFERENT enzymes and pathways - the other four options are all real reasons for that diversity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a metabolic cycle? Note: Shown are the substrates and products only; the enzymes are not shown.
questions.answerRationale: A cycle must return to its starting point: A→B→C→D→A closes the loop. The other options are linear or branching pathways, not cycles.

questions.stem: Only the reactants of a chemical reaction can get oxidized or reduced. For the reaction Ca + F2 à Ca2+ + 2F-,à CaF2, which of the following are oxidized and reduced?
questions.answerRationale: Ca goes from a neutral atom to Ca2+ (loses electrons = OXIDIZED); F goes from neutral to F- (gains an electron = REDUCED).

questions.stem: In the chemical reaction: pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA à acetyl-CoA + NADH+H+ + CO2, which of the reactants must have got reduced?
questions.answerRationale: NAD+ becomes NADH+H+ - it gained a hydride/electrons, so it was REDUCED. Pyruvate was oxidized (lost CO2 and electrons); CoA was neither oxidized nor reduced, just acylated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct example of ATP synthesis by substrate-level phosphorylation?
questions.answerRationale: GTP directly transferring its phosphate to ADP is a genuine substrate-level phosphorylation (direct donor-to-ADP transfer, as in the Krebs cycle’s succinyl-CoA step). (C) is just the generic ADP+Pi→ATP reaction common to BOTH substrate-level and oxidative phosphorylation, so it does not specifically illustrate substrate-level phosphorylation.

questions.stem: Which of the following agents pumps protons outside the membrane?

options.text: ETC complexes I, III, and IV.
Terminal electron acceptors (O2, CO2, S, NO3-, Fe3+, etc.).

questions.answerRationale: ETC Complexes I, III, and IV are the proton pumps that move H+ across the membrane. CoQ and cytochrome c are mobile electron carriers (they do not pump protons); F0F1 ATP synthase lets protons flow back IN, it does not pump them out.

questions.stem: Which of the following would stop the ATP synthesis by the ETC/ F0F1 ATP synthase?

options.text: Excess NADH and FADH2 in the cell.
More photons outside than inside the plasma membrane of a bacterium.
The membrane has a hole through which charged chemical substances may pass.
A coroplast inner membrane is used instead of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion.

questions.answerRationale: A hole in the membrane would let charged ions leak through and dissipate the proton gradient (the same way a chemical uncoupler works), stopping chemiosmotic ATP synthesis. The gradient itself (protons higher outside) is the normal, working state, not something that stops it.

questions.stem: Which of the following synthesizes ATP using the proton gradient?

options.text: A kinase enzyme using the reaction XPO4 + ADPà X+ ATP.
The F1 component of the F0F1 ATP synthase catalyzes the reaction ADP + PO4 à ATP.
The F0 component of the F0F1 ATP synthase catalyses the reaction XPO4 + ADPà X+ ATP.

questions.answerRationale: The F1 head of F0F1 ATP synthase is the part that actually catalyzes ADP + Pi → ATP, powered by protons flowing through F0 - this is literally "using the proton gradient." (A) and (C) describe substrate-level phosphorylation instead.

questions.stem: A FADH2 molecule donated its electrons to the ETC. Which of these will happen to the electrons?

options.text: It will go to CoQ to complex II to cytochrome c to complex IV to oxygen.
It will go to CoQ to complex I to complex III to cytochrome c to complex IV to oxygen.
It will go to CoQ to complex I to complex II to complex III to complex IV to oxygen to F0F1 ATP synthase.

questions.answerRationale: FADH2 donates electrons directly to Complex II (never Complex I, which is NADH-specific), and from there electrons flow to CoQ, cytochrome c, Complex IV, and finally oxygen - matching (A), the only option that excludes Complex I.

questions.stem: Which of these ways of ATP synthesis was neither aerobic nor anaerobic cellular respiration?

options.text: Used the ETC, the terminal electron acceptor was oxygen.
Used ETC, the terminal electron acceptor was an organic compound (i.e., CO2).
Used the ETC, the terminal electron acceptor was a molecule (Fe3+, NO3-, etc.) other than oxygen.
Lacked ETC, ATP was synthesized by glycolysis; electrons of NADH+H+ went to an organic compound.

questions.answerRationale: By definition, cellular respiration (aerobic or anaerobic) always uses an electron transport chain. This option has NO ETC at all - ATP comes only from glycolysis (substrate-level phosphorylation) and NADH’s electrons go to an organic molecule - that is fermentation, neither aerobic nor anaerobic respiration.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of fermentation?

options.text: Lactate + oxygen → acetic acid + CO2 + H2 gas.

questions.answerRationale: Pyruvate + NADH+H+ → Lactate + NAD+ regenerates NAD+ without an ETC - the defining feature of fermentation. (B) runs the reaction backward (consumes NAD+, does not regenerate it) and (C) uses oxygen, which is not fermentation at all.

questions.stem: Bacteria and fungi have a cell wall. How they utilize macromolecules (such as proteins and polysaccharides) as energy sources.

options.text: They do not use macromolecules as sources of nutrients.
They transport the macromolecules inside the cell and break them down.
They digest the macromolecules outside the cell, then bring the precursor molecules for ATP synthesis.

questions.answerRationale: Macromolecules are too large to cross the cell membrane, so bacteria/fungi secrete exoenzymes to digest them OUTSIDE the cell first, then transport the smaller breakdown products in for ATP synthesis.

questions.stem: Which of these sugar catabolic pathways must be in all cells because it creates ribose (and NADPH+H+)?
questions.answerRationale: The pentose phosphate pathway is defined by producing ribose-5-phosphate (needed by every cell for nucleotide/nucleic acid synthesis) and NADPH.

questions.stem: The cell needs NADH+H for ATP synthesis, and ATP and NADPH+H for anabolic reactions. Which of these sugar catabolic pathways generates both types of reducing power (i.e., NADH+H and NADPH+H) but no ATP?
questions.answerRationale: Among these four, the pentose phosphate pathway is the one built around generating reducing power rather than net ATP - it is the best fit for "reducing power but no ATP" among the listed pathways.

questions.stem: Which of these does the Krebs cycle NOT directly generate?
questions.answerRationale: The Krebs cycle’s substrate-level phosphorylation step directly makes GTP (option C, a real direct product) - GTP is then converted to ATP by a separate enzyme (nucleoside diphosphate kinase), so ATP itself is not directly generated by the cycle.

questions.stem: How many ATPs can be generated from one molecule of acetate if the cell has oxygen and all the enzymes of the Krebs cycle and ETC? Note: Assume that one NADH+H+= 3 ATPs and one FADH2 = 2 ATPs.
questions.answerRationale: One acetyl group through the Krebs cycle + ETC yields 3 NADH (×3=9 ATP) + 1 FADH2 (×2=2 ATP) + 1 GTP (=1 ATP) = 12 ATP.

questions.stem: In eukaryotes, which of the following reactions takes place in the matrix (i.e., the cytoplasm-equivalent) of mitochondria

options.text: ATP synthesis by F0F1 ATP synthase.

questions.answerRationale: The Krebs cycle enzymes are located in the mitochondrial matrix. Glycolysis is cytoplasmic; electron transport and F0F1 ATP synthase are both on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not in the matrix.

questions.stem: Giardia lamblia (a pathogenic protozoan) lacks mitochondria and some of the enzymes of the Krebs cycle. How does the organism synthesize ATP from sugars?
questions.answerRationale: Without mitochondria or Krebs cycle enzymes, the only ATP-generating mechanism left is substrate-level phosphorylation (as in glycolysis) - oxidative phosphorylation, aerobic respiration, and beta-oxidation all require the machinery Giardia lacks.

questions.stem: If completely burned, one mole (i.e., 180 gm) of glucose generates 686 kcal. E. coli burns glucose slowly and generates 32 moles of ATP; each mole of ATP= 7.3 kcal. How efficient is E. coli in energy recovery from glucose?

options.text: 28% Lipid, protein, and nucleic acid catabolism

questions.answerRationale: 32 mol ATP × 7.3 kcal/mol = 233.6 kcal captured, out of 686 kcal available = 233.6/686 ≈ 34%.

questions.stem: A molecule of triglyceride (also known as depot fat) was digested by a lipase enzyme. Which of these are expected products of the reaction?
questions.answerRationale: Lipase hydrolyzes the ester bonds of a triglyceride, directly releasing glycerol and (three) fatty acids - acyl-CoA, ATP/NADH, and phosphate are all later/unrelated products.

questions.stem: A fatty acid has 19 carbon atoms in its carbon skeleton. Through beta-oxidation, the fatty acid would generate _____________.
questions.answerRationale: Beta-oxidation removes 2 carbons at a time. An odd-numbered (19C) chain cannot divide evenly into 2-carbon units, so it ends in one 3-carbon propionyl-CoA plus eight 2-carbon acetyl-CoAs: (19-3)/2 = 8 acetyl-CoA + 1 propionyl-CoA.

questions.stem: Which of these is the SECOND step of protein catabolism?

options.text: Enzymatic removal of NH2, S, CO2 from amino acids
Opening of the ring structures in the R groups of amino acids
Oxidation of the organic acid skeleton of amino acids in the Krebs cycle.

questions.answerRationale: Protein catabolism proceeds: proteases break the protein into peptides (step 1), then peptidases break peptides into free amino acids (step 2), before amino group removal, R-group processing, and finally Krebs cycle oxidation.

questions.stem: Which of these is not directly generated from protein catabolism?
questions.answerRationale: Amino acids (and therefore proteins) contain no phosphorus in their basic structure, so phosphate is not a product of protein breakdown - CO2, ammonia, and sulfur compounds (from Cys/Met) all are.

questions.stem: Challenge question: Which of the following macromolecules does the cell NOT break and recycle on a regular basis?
questions.answerRationale: Genomic DNA is the cell’s permanent, protected genetic record - it is repaired, not routinely broken down and recycled for parts/energy the way carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and especially short-lived mRNA/tRNA are.

questions.stem: In nucleic acid catabolic activities, which of these enzymes remove PO4 groups from ribose sugars of a nucleotide?
questions.answerRationale: A nucleotidase removes the phosphate group from a nucleotide (converting it to a nucleoside) - by definition, the enzyme that "removes PO4 groups... of a nucleotide."

questions.stem: Which of the following usually offers most of the ATPs when a cell catabolizes nucleic acids?
questions.answerRationale: The ribose/deoxyribose sugar is the part of a nucleotide that can be fed into central sugar metabolism (e.g. via the pentose phosphate pathway) for real ATP-generating catabolism - the bases, phosphates, and phosphodiester linkages do not yield comparable usable energy.

questions.stem: Your mother-in-law served you a meal containing 8 grams of lipids, 10 grams of protein, 12 grams of carbohydrates, and 14 grams of DNA and RNA. Which of the food items came with the most total calories?
questions.answerRationale: Lipids have roughly double the caloric density of protein or carbohydrate (~9 kcal/g vs ~4 kcal/g), and nucleic acids are mostly non-caloric phosphate/base content - so even at a smaller mass (8g), the lipid portion contributes the most total calories.

questions.stem: How are ATPs used by the cells to conduct endergonic reactions?

options.text: The cell makes ATP to react with/activate one of the reactants, then uses the activated reactant to react with the other reactant to complete the endergonic reaction.
The cell breaks ATP to release heat energy, which serves as the activation energy for the endergonic reactions.
The method is yet to be fully elucidated.

questions.answerRationale: ATP couples to endergonic reactions by transferring its phosphate to (activating) one reactant, which then reacts with the other reactant to drive the otherwise-unfavorable reaction forward - not by releasing heat, which is not how controlled biological energy coupling works.
